items.q: JDBC and ODBC are:
options: Standard call-level APIs that let an application connect to a DBMS
items.explain: JDBC (Java) and ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) are standard APIs for embedding database access in application programs. Python uses a DB-API driver like mysql.connector.

items.q: Why use parameterised queries (e.g. `cur.execute(sql, (101, 'Riya'))`) instead of string concatenation?
items.explain: Placeholders (%s) keep data separate from SQL code, preventing SQL injection. The lifecycle is connect → cursor → execute → commit/rollback → fetch → close.

items.q: In the Python–MySQL pattern, what persists a change to the database?
items.explain: execute() sends the statement; conn.commit() makes the change permanent. conn.rollback() undoes it on error — wrapping the work in a transaction.

items.q: A database transaction is best described as:
options: A unit of work that is either fully completed or fully rolled back (all-or-nothing)
items.explain: A transaction is the smallest unit of work — a collection of operations that either all occur or none occur, ensuring data integrity.

items.q: Which ACID property ensures that once a transaction completes, its changes persist even after a system crash?
items.explain: Durability guarantees committed changes survive failures. It is enforced by the recovery system (via the log), which also enforces atomicity.

items.q: In a transfer of $50 from A to B, a crash after updating A but before updating B is prevented from corrupting the DB by which property?
items.explain: Atomicity ensures all-or-none: if the transaction fails midway, the recovery system uses the log to undo the partial change, so no money is lost.

items.q: Which ACID property is the responsibility of the concurrency-control system?
items.explain: Isolation (concurrent transactions appear to run one at a time) is enforced by the concurrency-control system. Atomicity and durability are handled by the recovery system via the log.

items.q: What does the read_item(X) operation do?
options: Copies data item X from the database into a main-memory buffer variable
items.explain: read(X) transfers X from the database (disk) into a buffer variable belonging to the transaction. write(X) copies the variable's value back to X (possibly buffered, flushed later).

items.q: Immediately after a transaction executes its final operation (but before commit checks pass), it is in which state?
items.explain: After the last operation the transaction is partially committed; concurrency/recovery checks run here. If they pass it reaches the commit point and becomes committed.

items.q: The system log is used primarily for:
options: Recovery — recording old/new values so changes can be undone or redone after a failure
items.explain: The log records each write's old and new values plus commit/abort markers, enabling the recovery system to undo uncommitted transactions and redo committed ones after a crash.

items.q: An aborted transaction is RESTARTED (as a new transaction) rather than killed when:
options: It had an internal logic error
The abort was due to an external cause (hardware/system error)
items.explain: External failures (hardware/system) are transient, so the transaction is restarted as new. Internal logic errors / bad input would just fail again, so the transaction is killed.

items.q: When one transaction's write is overwritten by another that read the old value, the anomaly is:
items.explain: Lost update: two transactions interleave so one's update overwrites the other's, which is lost. e.g. T1 writes X=3 but T2 (which read old X) writes X=8 over it.

items.q: A dirty read (temporary update problem) occurs when:
options: A transaction reads an uncommitted value that is later rolled back
items.explain: A dirty read happens when T2 reads data written but not yet committed by T1; if T1 rolls back, T2 has read a value that never validly existed.

items.q: The incorrect summary problem arises when:
options: A transaction reads its own writes
A transaction computes an aggregate while another updates items mid-scan
Two transactions write the same item
items.explain: Incorrect summary: an aggregate (sum/avg) is computed while another transaction updates some of the items being summed, so the result mixes old and new values.

items.q: The unrepeatable read problem is when a transaction:
options: Reads the same item twice and gets different values because another transaction changed it in between
items.explain: Unrepeatable read: T reads an item twice; another transaction modifies it between the two reads, so T sees two different values for the same item.

items.q: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms?
items.explain: READ COMMITTED reads only committed data (no dirty reads) but a re-read can still see updated values (non-repeatable) and newly inserted rows (phantoms).

items.q: Which isolation level avoids all three anomalies and is the SQL standard default?
items.explain: SERIALIZABLE is the strongest level, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms. It is the SQL default (though many systems default to READ COMMITTED for speed).

items.q: A phantom occurs when, between two reads of a transaction:
options: Another transaction INSERTS a new row matching the query's WHERE condition
items.explain: A phantom is a new row (inserted by another transaction) that satisfies a WHERE condition and appears in a re-run of the query — distinct from a non-repeatable read (a changed value).

items.q: REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads but still permits:
items.explain: REPEATABLE READ stops dirty and non-repeatable reads, but phantoms (newly inserted rows in a range query) can still occur; only SERIALIZABLE prevents those too.

items.q: Two operations in a schedule conflict if and only if:
options: They belong to different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write
They belong to the same transaction
items.explain: All three conditions must hold: different transactions, same data item, and at least one write. So R-W, W-R, W-W conflict; R-R never conflicts.

items.q: A serializable schedule is one that:
options: Runs transactions one at a time
Is a non-serial schedule equivalent to some serial schedule
items.explain: A serializable schedule allows concurrency but is equivalent in effect to some serial schedule, so it is consistent — combining correctness with better throughput.

items.q: A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by:
items.explain: Conflict serializability: a series of swaps of adjacent NON-conflicting operations turns the schedule into a serial one. Swapping non-conflicting ops never changes the result.

items.q: Which pair does NOT conflict?
items.explain: Two reads never conflict (neither is a write). The other pairs each have a write on the same item from different transactions, so they conflict.

items.q: In a precedence graph, an edge Ti → Tj is drawn when:
options: Ti and Tj are the same
Tj performs a conflicting operation AFTER Ti on the same item (W-R, R-W, or W-W)
items.explain: An edge Ti → Tj means a conflicting operation of Tj follows one of Ti on the same data item (e.g. wi(X) then rj(X)), forcing Ti before Tj in any equivalent serial order.

items.q: A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph:
items.explain: Acyclic ⇒ conflict serializable (and a topological sort gives the equivalent serial order). A cycle ⇒ NOT conflict serializable.

items.q: For an acyclic precedence graph, the equivalent serial order is found by:
options: Finding the node with most edges
Topological sort — repeatedly removing a node with in-degree 0
items.explain: A topological sort gives the serial order: repeatedly pick a node with in-degree 0, output it, and remove it. That removal order is the equivalent serial schedule.

items.q: Why is serializability testing (precedence graph) not used at runtime by the DBMS?
options: It requires the whole schedule after the fact; instead a protocol (like 2PL) guarantees only serializable schedules are produced
items.explain: Testing needs the complete schedule. Instead the DBMS uses a protocol such as two-phase locking that guarantees conflict-serializable schedules by construction. The graph is for proving protocols and solving problems.

items.q: Two schedules are view equivalent if they have the same initial reads, the same read-from relationships, and:
options: The same final write (last writer) of each data item
items.explain: View equivalence requires all three: same initial reads, same read-from (who-reads-whose-write), and same final writer of each item.

items.q: The relationship between conflict- and view-serializable schedules is:
options: Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable, but not vice-versa
items.explain: Conflict-serializable ⊂ view-serializable. View-serializable schedules that aren't conflict-serializable always contain a blind write. Hierarchy: serial ⊂ conflict-SR ⊂ view-SR ⊂ all.

items.q: A blind write is:
options: A write to an item with no prior read of that item by the same transaction
items.explain: A blind write writes an item the transaction never read. Blind writes are what make some schedules view-serializable but not conflict-serializable.

items.q: Why is conflict serializability emphasised over view serializability in practice?
options: Testing conflict serializability is a cheap cycle check, whereas testing view serializability is NP-complete
items.explain: Conflict serializability is tested with a simple precedence-graph cycle check; view serializability testing is NP-complete. Protocols enforce the easier-to-guarantee conflict serializability.

items.q: A shared (S) lock allows the holder to:
items.explain: A shared lock permits reading only; many transactions can hold S-locks on an item simultaneously. An exclusive (X) lock permits read AND write, held by one transaction.

items.q: In the lock-compatibility matrix, which combination is compatible (can be held concurrently)?
items.explain: Only Shared–Shared is compatible (many readers). Any combination involving an exclusive lock is incompatible, so a writer must wait for all other locks to release.

items.q: Deadlock between two transactions is resolved by:
options: Rolling back one of the transactions
items.explain: When two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds, one must be rolled back to break the cycle. MySQL detects deadlocks automatically and rolls back a victim.

items.q: A transaction waiting for an exclusive lock being repeatedly overtaken by shared-lock grants is an example of:
items.explain: Starvation: a continuous stream of compatible shared-lock requests can indefinitely delay an exclusive-lock request. FIFO granting in the lock table prevents it.

items.q: In two-phase locking (2PL), the two phases are:
options: Growing phase (acquire locks, no release) and shrinking phase (release locks, no acquire)
items.explain: Growing: only acquire locks. Shrinking: only release. Once a transaction releases any lock it cannot acquire new ones. The lock point is the end of the growing phase.

items.q: What does basic 2PL guarantee — and not guarantee?
options: Guarantees conflict serializability but NOT freedom from deadlock
items.explain: 2PL guarantees conflict-serializable schedules (serialized in lock-point order) but transactions following 2PL can still deadlock, which must be handled separately.

items.q: How does rigorous 2PL differ from strict 2PL?
options: Strict holds all EXCLUSIVE locks till commit; rigorous holds ALL locks (S and X) till commit
items.explain: Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit/abort (recoverable, no cascading rollback). Rigorous 2PL holds ALL locks until commit, serializing transactions in commit order. Most DBs use rigorous 2PL.

items.q: In 2PL, upgrading a shared lock to an exclusive lock (S → X) is allowed only in the:
items.explain: Upgrading (S→X) acquires more locking power, so it's a growing-phase action. Downgrading (X→S) releases power, so it's a shrinking-phase action.

items.q: Why does 2PL guarantee conflict serializability (proof idea)?
options: If the precedence graph had a cycle, some transaction must have acquired a lock after releasing one — violating the two-phase rule
items.explain: A cycle in the precedence graph would require a transaction to lock after unlocking, which 2PL forbids. Hence 2PL schedules are acyclic, i.e. conflict serializable.

items.q: NoSQL stands for and emphasises:
options: Not Only SQL; schema-less, scalable, available storage of unstructured data
items.explain: NoSQL = Not Only SQL — non-tabular, schema-less databases emphasising scalability, availability, replication and performance over immediate consistency and rich query languages.

items.q: Which is the correct NoSQL category for Neo4j?
items.explain: Neo4j is a graph database. The four categories: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, HBase), graph (Neo4j).

items.q: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system with replication can guarantee at most how many of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance?
items.explain: CAP: you cannot guarantee all three simultaneously — at most two. Since partitions are unavoidable, the practical choice is between consistency and availability.

items.q: Most NoSQL systems, in CAP terms, choose to favour:
options: Availability + partition tolerance, accepting eventual consistency
items.explain: NoSQL systems typically prioritise availability and partition tolerance (A+P), adopting eventual consistency, whereas traditional SQL/ACID systems prioritise consistency.

items.q: Sharding in NoSQL systems refers to:
options: Partitioning records across multiple nodes to distribute load
items.explain: Sharding partitions the records across nodes for load balancing; combined with replication it improves both availability and load distribution.

items.q: Redis is best described as:
items.explain: Redis is an open-source, in-memory key-value store (RAM for speed, disk for persistence) — a persisted hash map, schema-less and very fast.

items.q: Which Redis data structure is ideal for a real-time leaderboard?
items.explain: A Sorted Set keeps members ordered by a score (ties broken lexicographically) — perfect for leaderboards/rankings via ZADD/ZRANGE/ZREVRANGE/ZRANK.

items.q: Which Redis command sets a timeout after which a key is automatically deleted?
items.explain: EXPIRE key seconds sets a timeout (used for caching/sessions). TTL reads the remaining time; PERSIST removes the timeout; DEL deletes immediately.

items.q: Which is a limitation of Redis?
options: Data is held in RAM (expensive, risk of loss on crash) and it's not suited to complex joins/aggregations
items.explain: Redis keeps everything in RAM (expensive, possible data loss on crash, manual eviction) and is optimised for key lookups, not complex joins or aggregations.

items.q: In a Redis key like `user:101`, the colon (`:`) is used to:
items.explain: The colon conventionally denotes hierarchy/namespacing (e.g. PES:Department, user:session:123), helping organise the flat key space. Keys must be unique.

items.q: In Neo4j, what do nodes and relationships represent?
options: Nodes = entities (people, things); relationships = directed connections between them
items.explain: Neo4j's storage model is nodes + relationships. Nodes represent entities (with labels and properties); directed relationships (with a type) connect them.

items.q: The key advantage of Neo4j over a relational database is:
options: Efficient handling of highly connected data (fast traversals vs costly JOINs)
items.explain: Graph traversals follow direct relationship pointers, so relationship-heavy queries (friends-of-friends, recommendations) are far faster than rebuilding many relational JOINs.

items.q: Neo4j's query language is:
items.explain: Cypher (CQL) is Neo4j's declarative pattern-matching language: CREATE for nodes/relationships, MATCH ... RETURN for queries; → shows relationship direction.

items.q: A difference between Neo4j and the ER model is:
options: ER relationships are directed; Neo4j's are not
In Neo4j relationships are directed and a node may have NO label; in ER every entity must have a type
Neo4j is only a design tool
items.explain: Neo4j relationships are directed and a node may have zero labels; in ER, relationships are undirected and every entity belongs to an entity type. Neo4j is a real DBMS; ER is a design tool.

items.q: A vector database primarily retrieves data by:
items.explain: Vector databases store high-dimensional embeddings and retrieve by similarity (semantic meaning), enabling semantic search, recommendations, and RAG — beyond exact matching.

items.q: An embedding is:
options: A vector produced by a model that captures the semantic meaning of text/image/audio
items.explain: An embedding is a numerical vector generated by an embedding model (e.g. OpenAI, Google) that captures semantic meaning, so similar objects map to nearby vectors.

items.q: Which metric measures similarity by the cosine of the angle between two vectors (1 = very similar, 0 = unrelated)?
items.explain: Cosine similarity = cosine of the angle between vectors: 1 (same direction) = very similar, 0 (orthogonal) = unrelated, −1 = opposite. Euclidean distance is the other common metric.

items.q: HNSW is an example of a(n):
options: Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) vector index using a hierarchical graph
items.explain: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a hierarchical graph for fast, memory-efficient approximate nearest-neighbour search. IVFPQ is another (inverted file + product quantization).

items.q: How does vector (semantic) search differ from full-text search (FTS)?
options: FTS is semantic; vector is lexical
FTS matches words via an inverted index; vector search matches meaning via embeddings and a vector index
Vector search only works on numbers
items.explain: FTS matches tokens/stems using an inverted index and ranks by TF-IDF/BM25; vector search matches semantic meaning using embeddings and a vector index (HNSW/IVF), handling synonyms and context.
